title: Вечеринка для одной звезды  (A Party for One Star)

segments.t: After the shift, all the other cooks boycott the celebration, and a tired Vika prepares to head home as well. When Aleksandr smoothly confesses that he threw the entire party just to be alone with her, Max pulls the new chef aside and warns him to stay away from Vika.
Да нет, что-то не хочется.
Да настроения нет.
Я очень устала.
Я поеду домой.
Виктория Сергеевна, вы главная звезда сегодняшнего вечера.
Вся эта вечеринка, она устроена только для вас.
Нет, сегодня ты никуда не пойдешь.
Сможешь тебя на минутку? Да?
Ты что творишь?
Да о чем?
А Вики не трогай ее, понял?
Тебе-то какое дело?
Она моя.
Let's replay the exchange and look closely at each Russian phrase.
Да нет, что-то не хочется.
'No, I do not really feel like it.' The meaning hinges on 'yes' working together with 'feel like it' in spoken Russian.
Да настроения нет.
'I am just not in the mood.' In Russian, the idea of 'yes' flows naturally into 'there is no' without extra filler words. Vika answers right away.
Я очень устала.
'I am very tired.' The meaning hinges on 'I' working together with 'are tired' in spoken Russian.
Я поеду домой.
'I am going to head home.' The grammar packs 'I' and 'home' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
Виктория Сергеевна, вы главная звезда сегодняшнего вечера.
'Viktoriya Sergeyevna, you are the main star of tonight's evening.' Chef Viktor chooses the respectful plural 'you' alongside 'evening' to keep a polite distance. Vika answers right away.
Вся эта вечеринка, она устроена только для вас.
'This whole party was arranged solely for you.' The grammar packs 'whole' and 'you' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
Нет, сегодня ты никуда не пойдешь.
'No, you are not going anywhere tonight.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'there is no' and finishing on 'will go'.
Сможешь тебя на минутку? Да?
'Can I have a word with you for a minute? Yes?' Notice how Russian expresses 'will you be able' and 'yes' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Vika answers right away.
Ты что творишь?
'What do you think you are doing?' Vika raises the pitch on 'are doing' to turn the phrase into a direct spoken question.
Да о чем?
'What are you talking about?' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'yes' before landing on 'what'.
А Вики не трогай ее, понял?
'Keep your hands off Vika, got it?' The grammar packs 'and' and 'understood?' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Vika answers right away.
Тебе-то какое дело?
'What business is it of yours?' The meaning hinges on 'to you' working together with 'matter' in spoken Russian.
Она моя.
'She is mine.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'she' and finishing on 'my'. Let's hear the complete conversation once more.
